result: A systematic review identified 19 studies with suitable contact data from LIC, LMIC, and UMIC settings, with individual-level data obtained from 16 studies. All included studies scored above 65% on the AXIS risk of bias tool, suggesting good or fair quality.
evaluation: Claims C20-C25 describe the systematic review methodology and quality assessment. The search strategy, inclusion criteria, income classification, number of identified studies, and quality assessment are clearly documented with appropriate detail and citations to data sources.

result: The meta-analysis included 28,503 participants and 413,069 contacts across 27 surveys. The sample comprised 47.5% males, 30.1% aged under 15 years, and 7.2% aged over 65 years. Most participants (83.4%) reported weekday contacts. Household size varied substantially by income setting, with 63.2% of LIC/LMIC respondents living in large households (6+ members) compared to 35.9% in UMICs and 4.9% in HICs.
evaluation: Claims C3 and C26-C35 provide descriptive statistics of the study sample. These are directly reported data from the meta-analysis with clear numerical values and appropriate stratification by income level. The data are internally consistent and well-documented.

result: The median number of daily contacts was 9 (IQR 5-17) across all studies and similar across income strata (LIC/LMIC=10, UMIC=8, HIC=9). However, there was large variation across studies (range 4-24 contacts), and diary-based surveys reported higher contact rates than interview/questionnaire-based surveys across all income strata.
evaluation: Claims C36-C39 report descriptive findings on contact rates. The data are clearly presented with appropriate measures of central tendency and variability. The observation about methodological differences (diary vs. interview) is important for interpretation and is supported by the data presented in Table 1.

result: School-aged children had the highest number of daily contacts across all income settings, consistent with previous HIC studies. However, age-related patterns differed by income level: contact rates declined with age in UMICs and HICs (adjCRR for 65+ vs. <15 years: UMIC=0.67, HIC=0.57), but not in LICs/LMICs (adjCRR=0.94, 95%CrI: 0.89-1.00), where older adults maintained similar contact rates to younger individuals.
evaluation: Claims C40-C43, C123-C124, and C4-C5 describe age-related contact patterns. The findings are supported by statistical analysis with appropriate effect sizes and credible intervals. The contrast between income settings is clearly demonstrated and represents a key finding of the study.

result: Gender effects on contact frequency varied by income setting. In LICs/LMICs, men made more daily contacts than women (adjCRR=1.17, 95%CrI: 1.15-1.20), but there was no gender effect in UMICs (CRR=1.01) or HICs (CRR=0.99).
evaluation: Claims C125-C127 and C10 report gender-specific contact patterns stratified by income level. The statistical analysis is appropriate with effect sizes and credible intervals provided. The contrasting effects across income strata are clearly demonstrated.

result: Students aged 5-18 made more daily contacts than non-students of the same age across all income strata (adjCRR: LIC/LMIC=1.26, UMIC=1.18, HIC=1.54). Similarly, employed adults had higher contact rates than unemployed adults across all settings (adjCRR: LIC/LMIC=1.17, UMIC=1.07, HIC=1.60).
evaluation: Claims C116-C117 describe the effects of student and employment status on contact rates. The findings are supported by appropriate statistical analysis with effect sizes and credible intervals across all income strata, demonstrating consistent patterns.

result: Household size was a key determinant of contact frequency across all settings. Median household size decreased with increasing country income (LIC/LMIC=7, UMIC=5, HIC=3), consistent with global data. Individuals in large households (6+ members) had 1.47-2.58 times more daily contacts than those living alone. LIC/LMIC households were more intergenerational, with 59.4% of those aged 65+ living in households of 6+ members, compared to 17.5% in UMICs and 2.2% in HICs.
evaluation: Claims C6-C7, C65-C70, and C118-C122 describe household size effects on contact patterns. The findings are well-supported by statistical analysis with appropriate effect sizes across income strata. The comparison with global UN data (C66) provides external validation. The intergenerational household structure findings are clearly documented.

result: Contact location varied substantially by income setting. Of 314,235 contacts with known location, 42.7% occurred at home overall, but this proportion was highest in LICs/LMICs (68.3%) and lowest in HICs (37.0%). Conversely, work and school contacts were more frequent in HICs (14.6% and 11.3%) than LICs/LMICs (3.9% and 5.2%). The number of home contacts was driven by household size, with larger households in LIC/LMICs associated with more, longer-lasting, and more physical contacts. Males made a higher proportion of work contacts than females across all income strata, with the largest difference in LICs/LMICs.
evaluation: Claims C57-C64, C8-C9, and C48-C52 describe contact location patterns. The findings are supported by substantial data (>314,000 contacts) with clear proportions reported. The stratification by income level reveals important differences in where contacts occur, which has implications for disease transmission and intervention strategies.

result: Physical contact patterns varied by age, gender, income setting, and location. The mean percentage of physical contacts was 56.0% overall and highest for LICs/LMICs (64.5%). Physical contacts were less common among adults than children (ORs: 0.22-0.48), but increased again in those aged 80+. Gender effects were reversed across income settings: in LICs/LMICs, women had more physical contacts than men (adjOR=0.81), while in UMICs and HICs, men had more physical contacts (adjOR=1.13 and 1.09, respectively). Physical contacts were most common at home (70.4%), followed by schools (58.5%), community (55.7%), and work (33.6%). Larger household size was associated with more physical contacts across all settings.
evaluation: Claims C71-C92 describe physical contact patterns with data from 20,910 participants. The findings are supported by appropriate statistical analysis with odds ratios and credible intervals. The contrasting gender effects across income settings and the location-specific patterns are clearly demonstrated and represent important findings for understanding transmission risk.

result: Contact duration patterns varied by age, gender, income setting, and location. Among 22,822 participants, 63.2% of contacts lasted ≥1 hour, with the highest proportion in UMICs (76.0%) and lowest in LICs/LMICs (53.1%). Duration decreased with age in UMICs and HICs but less so in LICs/LMICs. Gender effects varied: males made longer contacts in UMICs (adjOR=1.11) but not in LICs/LMICs or HICs. Contacts were shorter on weekends in LICs/LMICs and HICs but not UMICs. Longer contacts were most common at home (72.7%), followed by schools (67.9%), community (47.0%), and work (44.0%). Student status significantly affected duration only in HICs (adjOR=1.18). Larger household size was associated with longer contacts across all income strata.
evaluation: Claims C93-C109 describe contact duration patterns with data from 22,822 participants. The findings are supported by appropriate statistical analysis with odds ratios and credible intervals. The income-specific and location-specific patterns are clearly demonstrated and provide important insights into transmission risk factors.

result: Mixing patterns were assortative by both gender and age across all income strata. However, age assortativity was lowest in LICs/LMICs, where only 29% of adult contacts were with the same age group, compared to HICs where 51.4% of older adult contacts were with the same age group. This pattern is consistent with household structure differences: nearly two-thirds of participants aged 65+ in LIC/LMIC surveys lived in large, intergenerational households (6+ members), compared to only 2% in HICs.
evaluation: Claims C110-C115, C46-C47, and C44-C45 describe mixing patterns by age and gender. The findings are supported by data from 12 studies (gender) and 8 studies (age). The lower age assortativity in LICs/LMICs is clearly linked to household structure differences, providing a coherent explanation for the observed patterns.

result: Differences in contact patterns between income settings have material consequences for respiratory pathogen spread and NPI effectiveness. The findings suggest that NPI effectiveness estimates derived primarily from European data may have limited generalizability to non-European settings with different contact structures. Physical contacts generally declined with age except in the very old, potentially reflecting dependency and care needs.
evaluation: Claims C11, C56, and C55 present interpretations and implications of the findings. These are reasonable inferences supported by the documented differences in contact patterns across settings. The limitation regarding generalizability of European NPI estimates is appropriately cautious and supported by citation to relevant work.

result: All analyses were conducted in a Bayesian framework using Stan with uninformative priors, implemented in R via the brms package. Analyses were stratified by three income strata (LICs and LMICs combined) and included random effects by study to account for heterogeneity.
evaluation: Claims C128-C131 describe the statistical methodology. The approach is appropriate for the data structure (hierarchical with multiple studies) and clearly documented with software citations. The use of random effects to account for study heterogeneity is methodologically sound.

result: All collated surveys were conducted prior to the SARS-CoV-2 pandemic. Previous work has documented significant, dynamic alterations to contact patterns in response to COVID-19 control measures, but data on contact patterns during COVID-19 remains sparse and available for only limited settings.
evaluation: Claims C132-C135 describe the temporal context and limitations of the study. The timing of surveys is clearly stated, and the discussion of COVID-19-related changes is appropriately supported by citations. The acknowledgment of data sparsity during the pandemic is accurate.

result: Prospective diary-based reporting, which is less affected by recall bias, can lead to higher reported contact numbers. The relatively high contact rates in HICs may be explained by the predominant use of diary methods (all but two HIC surveys). Median daily contacts were higher in diary-based surveys compared to interview/questionnaire-based surveys across all income strata.
evaluation: Claims C136-C138 and C39 discuss methodological effects on contact reporting. The relationship between survey method and reported contacts is supported by both citation to previous work and the current study's data. The inference about HIC contact rates is reasonable given the methodological distribution.

result: The study highlights the need for unified contact definitions and standardized data collection practices to improve data quality and enable more robust conclusions. It also emphasizes the limited work undertaken to understand contact patterns in LICs and middle-income countries, which is vital for informing control strategies.
evaluation: Claims C139-C140 present conclusions and recommendations based on the systematic review findings. The call for standardization is justified by the observed methodological heterogeneity. The identification of research gaps in LICs/middle-income countries is directly supported by the systematic review results showing limited available studies.

result: Transmission of respiratory pathogens depends on contact patterns across populations. Most previous analyses have focused on high-income settings, despite evidence that contact patterns differ systematically across settings with material consequences for transmission dynamics. Previous reviews primarily explored total contact numbers and age/sex distribution, while recent work has emphasized the importance of contact characteristics (location, duration, physical contact) in determining transmission risk.
evaluation: Claims C1-C2 and C12-C19 provide background context supported by appropriate citations to previous work. These establish the rationale for the study by identifying gaps in existing knowledge and the importance of contact characteristics beyond simple counts.
